transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-12 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Leah Ortiz (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (BlueCrest ML Eng), Sana Ahmed (BlueCrest Head of Data), Tom Li (BlueCrest Infra), Maya Chen (BlueCrest PM)

Auto-summary (auto): discuss tail latency and sharding strategy for rerank.

[00:00] Ethan Park: Hey everyone thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Ethan, AE at Redwood. Leah is our solutions engineer, she's gonna drive the technical pieces.
[00:18] Raj Patel: Thanks Ethan, yeah happy to be here. We're trying to figure out how to keep tail latency down when we do a two-stage rerank—dense vector search then a Model-based reranker.
[00:30] Leah Ortiz: Great, can you describe your current stack and traffic shape? approximate QPS, embedding dims, types of queries?
[00:42] Raj Patel: Sure. Right now we have a hybrid search setup: sparse BM25 prefilter then dense vector recall using an on-prem Milvus cluster that's sharded by namespace. Embeddings are 768-dim from an in-house model, and production traffic varies, baseline 30 qps but peaks around 140 QPS during daytime. Typical request is embed + topK 200 recall then rerank top 20.
[01:05] Leah Ortiz: Ok so end-to-end includes embedding generation, nearest neighbor retrieval, then reranker scoring—so three moving pieces. Are you doing embedding generation in the request path or pre-computing?
[01:15] Sana Ahmed: We precompute for docs, but for queries we generate on the fly. Query latency for embedding is about 60-80ms on our nodes. The big variance is in retrieval tail—some shards go hot and you see p95 blow up.
[01:30] Tom Li: We shard by customer segment but the shard distribution is kind of skewed; some user cohorts hit large shards.
[01:36] Ethan Park: Typical. So the questions I want to focus on today are: can Redwood's runtime reduce tail latency through routing, caching, and a Dedicated capacity configuration; and whether an on-prem/private deployment is necessary given your compliance needs.
[01:49] Raj Patel: Right, security is a factor. We are SOC2 compliant, need KMS integration and audit logs. Also prefer VPC peering for Private deployment.
[01:58] Leah Ortiz: We support VPC/private options with customer-managed KMS and audit logs; for Hosted we offer encryption at rest and in transit, but we know some customers require full Private.
[02:09] Maya Chen: Timeline wise, we want a pilot in Q3. If the pilot meets our p95 and cost targets, we'll move to a Dedicated commit.
[02:18] Ethan Park: Good. Can you share your p95 target?
[02:20] Maya Chen: Ideally under 450ms for the full loop (embed + approx search + rerank).
[02:27] Leah Ortiz: That's ambitious at 150 QPS, but doable with the right batching, KV/prefix caching, and sharded routing. A couple clarifying Qs: what's your reranker model (size) and where is it hosted?
[02:39] Raj Patel: It's a distilled cross-encoder, roughly 200M params, we serve in our infra on GPU instances. Reranker latency is about 80-120ms per 20 candidates depending on batch.
[02:51] Leah Ortiz: Ok. Some levers to reduce tail: 1) reduce recall topK (we can recommend an eval to see how topK affects quality), 2) deploy Redwood Dedicated close to your VPC or use private to remove network hops, 3) enable automatic shard-aware routing to avoid scattering queries across all shards, 4) use prefix/KV cache for repeated queries.
[03:11] Raj Patel: Shard-aware routing—can you explain?
[03:13] Leah Ortiz: Sure. If your vector DB has metadata sharding like user namespace, Redwood can be configured to route to the subset of replicas that own the relevant partition. That avoids fan-out to all shards which reduces tail.
[03:24] Tom Li: That sounds like we'd need the DB to expose partition mapping or a routing key. We can do that.
[03:30] Ethan Park: Another lever is reranker offload: run approximate rerank on CPU or use a smaller cross-encoder for the warm path and full model for fallback. That helps with cost too.
[03:41] Raj Patel: We worry about quality drop with smaller rerankers. Our evaluation metric is MRR and top1 accuracy.
[03:47] Leah Ortiz: We usually run an offline eval to quantify the trade-off—often a 10% drop in MRR buys a 2-3x tail latency improvement. We'll share an eval template.
[03:58] Sana Ahmed: About dimensionality—we're considering moving to 512 dims from 768 to reduce index size. How will that affect recall?
[04:07] Leah Ortiz: Lower dims reduce index size and can improve throughput and cache efficiency, but there's a diminishing return on quality. We'll propose running an A/B eval with your dataset and both dims to measure the delta.
[04:20] Raj Patel: For our workload, storage and throughput matter a lot because we replicate across 3 regions. Storage savings compound.
[04:28] Ethan Park: Right. For Dedicated, we can propose shard counts and NVMe-backed caches; for Private you control replication. Hosted can still do region routing but private gives more network determinism.
[04:40] Maya Chen: What about fallback behavior if a shard is unhealthy? We need graceful degradation rather than full errors.
[04:47] Leah Ortiz: Redwood supports automatic fallback to a compatible model variant and partial results. For vector DB failures, we can reduce fanout or fall back to cached results for a short TTL.
[04:58] Tom Li: Ok. Can Redwood run a benchmark against a snapshot of our DB that we share? We'd like numbers: median, p95, p99 for the end-to-end pipeline at 50/100/150 qps.
[05:08] Leah Ortiz: Yes, we have a benchmark harness. If you provide a sample corpus and a synthetic QPS trace, we can run it in a Dedicated sandbox. We also suggest testing hybrid search (sparse + dense) since your prefilter is BM25.
[05:21] Raj Patel: Good. On the vector DB side, we're using Milvus 2.x with IVF-PQ indexes for recall. Any gotchas?
[05:28] Leah Ortiz: IVF-PQ is fine but PQ adds quantization error—re-ranking can fix residual errors but increases CPU. Also PQ can make distance computations cheaper but sometimes increases variance. For rerank-heavy pipelines you might prefer HNSW on smaller dims or hybrid indexing.
[05:44] Ethan Park: I'll add that we often recommend HNSW for low-latency retrieval at the cost of larger index size. If storage is an issue, a hybrid approach—IVF-PQ for cold partitions and HNSW for hot partitions—can help.
[05:57] Sana Ahmed: What about quantized model serving? If we quantize the reranker to INT8, can we keep quality?
[06:03] Leah Ortiz: Quantization helps latency and memory but you need to validate. For the cross-encoder you may see minor quality drop; we can include quantized variants in the pilot.
[06:12] Raj Patel: Network overhead has been a surprise—some of our latency comes from cross-region calls between the embed service and the DB.
[06:19] Tom Li: That's why we're exploring Dedicated in-region or Private to eliminate cross-cloud hops.
[06:24] Ethan Park: For Dedicated, we can colocate inference with the DB and use fast local network fabric. Also Redwood's runtime supports colocated KV caches to reduce repeated nearest neighbor overhead.
[06:36] Raj Patel: About cost—do you have ballpark numbers for 150 QPS rerank with Dedicated?
[06:42] Ethan Park: We'll send a tailored pricing sheet, but rough math: if most of the work is embedding + retrieval (and reranker is a smaller part), Dedicated commit for a pool sized for 150 QPS of embeddings + 20 GPU reranker instances will be competitive versus self-host. We'll include per-token and per-inference comparisons.
[06:58] Maya Chen: Any compliance docs we can review? SOC2, PCI (not necessary), KMS integrations?
[07:05] Ethan Park: Yes, we'll share our security pack with SOC2 docs, encryption details, audit log samples, and our Private deployment spec for KMS/HSM.
[07:12] Raj Patel: One more question—how does Redwood handle model rollouts? We need to A/B test new embed models and be able to rollback quickly.
[07:20] Leah Ortiz: We have rollout policies, canary hosts, and version pinning per route. You can route a percentage of traffic to new embeddings and monitor quality delta via eval hooks.
[07:30] Raj Patel: Good.
[07:32] Speaker 1: (mumble) when you said prefix cache is that per-query or per-user?
[07:37] Leah Ortiz: Good Q. Prefix/KV caching is configurable—per-query fingerprinting for short-term repeats, or user/session-level caches for personalization.
[07:45] Maya Chen: For the pilot, what dataset size do you need to be meaningful?
[07:50] Leah Ortiz: For tail-latency characterization, a few thousand queries with realistic skew and a snapshot of ~5-10k docs is enough for an initial run. We'll then scale to larger corpora for production sizing.
[07:59] Tom Li: We'll prepare a scrubbed snapshot.
[08:03] Ethan Park: Great. Let's talk about the benchmark plan—Leah?
[08:06] Leah Ortiz: Plan: 1) BlueCrest provides snapshot + query trace, 2) Redwood runs runs (sic) three scenarios: Hosted (region-local), Dedicated colocation, Private (if requested), 3) measure median/p95/p99 for embed, search, and rerank separately and end-to-end, 4) share CSVs and a short analysis. We also include a sharding config suggestion.
[08:28] Raj Patel: For the sharding config, can you recommend shard counts per region and replica factor?
[08:33] Leah Ortiz: We'll recommend target shard sizes (~50-200M vectors per shard depending on index type), and a replication factor of 2-3 for HA. We'll include guidance for hot-shard mitigation (rebalancing or adaptive routing).
[08:46] Sana Ahmed: How about observability—tracing and span context across the embed, DB, and reranker?
[08:52] Leah Ortiz: Redwood supports tracing hooks and per-token latency breakdowns in the Console. For Private deployments we can forward spans to your tracing backend.
[09:02] Raj Patel: Any customer references using a similar stack?
[09:06] Ethan Park: We can share a contact from healthcare who runs a heavy rerank flow with Dedicated—will send intro if that's helpful.
[09:13] Maya Chen: That would help.
[09:15] Ethan Park: Ok let's summarize: action items and timeline. Leah to run benchmark and share by next week. I'll send pricing and security pack. BlueCrest to provide scrubbed data and QPS traces.
[09:26] Tom Li: Sounds good.
[09:28] Raj Patel: Quick note—we may want a technical deep-dive after benchmarks if we need to tune indices.
[09:34] Leah Ortiz: Yep, happy to do that. We'll also include a recommended experiment matrix (dims, index type, topK).
[09:43] Maya Chen: Any immediate blockers on our side? Not really, we'll coordinate data sharing and NDA if needed.
[09:50] Ethan Park: We'll include an NDA template in the packet. Anything else?
[09:55] Speaker 2: no, thanks
[09:57] Ethan Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with next steps.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: some overlapped talk and a few proper-noun mis-transcribes (Milvus, HNSW, KMS), quality medium.
